newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA POWER COMPANY TO INVEST $370 MLN BY 1999.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA POWER COMPANY TO INVEST $370 MLN BY 1999.

text.p: Bulgaria's National Electricity Company (NEC) plans to invest up to $370 million by the end of 1998 to revitalise the country's ageing power installations, its deputy executive director said on Thursday.

"The country's energy sector has been deprived of investment for the last 5-6 years and this year we are planning investment of $80 million to $120 million," Dimcho Ivanov, who is also a deputy chairman of the NEC executive board, told a news conference.
Ivanov said plans were to invest $250 million in 1998.
He said the investment would be financed by credits from international financial institutions and the company's own funds. He gave no further details.
The new investment would go towards the construction of two more hydroelectric power units of the Chaira pumped storage plant, which will provide 432 megawatts at peak capacity.
Another part will be for safety reconstruction of all six units of the 3,760-megawatt nuclear power plant at Kozloduy, which provides 40 percent of the country's electricity.
The third main target of the investment will be building a sulphur reduction installation for a new coal-fired power plant at the Maritsa East Two power complex in southern Bulgaria.
The NEC called a tender for building the installation last year and a contract with the winner is expected to be signed within two to three months, Ivanov said.

Bulgaria, which lacks energy resources and imports more than 80 percent of its raw materials, relies on antiquated thermal power plants for half of its electricity. The coal it produces is mainly low quality lignite.

The amount will be topped up partly by collecting debt owed to the company of some 40 billion levs, mostly from the industrial sector, said the new chairman of the NEC executive board, Vassil Anastasov.
He said the company had prepared a proposal for criminalising electricity theft and would deposit it in parliament as soon as it starts work next month.

The company, which is among the 70 state-owned firms barred from drawing credits from local trade banks until they stabilise their finances, also relies on its restructuring programme, aimed at boosting production at lower cost.

The NEC also hopes to increase electricity sales to neighbouring countries. "Now we export electricity to Turkey and we have a contract for electricity exports with Greece for several months," Anastasov said. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-91188
